scenarios.title: Look beyond the loose puck
scenarios.objective: Locate an outlet and approaching pressure before planning a retrieval.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are approaching a loose puck near the side wall. F2 is an outlet toward the middle; D1 is approaching from up ice. No player has recovered the puck yet.
cues: The puck is loose beside the wall.
F2 is away from the wall.
D1 approaches from the up-ice side.

questions.prompt: What is true about possession at this freeze?

options.text: YOU already control the puck
The puck is loose
D1 has made a pass

questions.explanation: The puck is drawn away from every blade and has no owner.

questions.prompt: Which two things would help YOU plan the pickup?

options.text: Where F2 is available
The direction D1 approaches from
Only the loose puck, without checking the players

questions.explanation: An outlet and the approaching pressure inform the next action; neither guarantees a successful pickup.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested retrieval plan.

options.text: Find the pressure and outlet
Approach and control the loose puck
Check whether the outlet is still available

questions.explanation: This is a simple discussion routine. Real scanning may repeat throughout the approach.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an approach point that leaves a view toward F2.
questions.explanation: The example approaches on the middle side of the puck and short of the wall, with F2 in the wider scene. Other controlled approaches can preserve an outlet.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 closes the middle outlet before the pickup. What could YOU reconsider?

options.text: Use the same middle pass regardless
Check another exit before committing
Assume F2 has already received

questions.explanation: The old outlet may no longer be useful. A turn, protected hold or different pass depends on the new pressure.

questions.prompt: What would you want to see again just before touching this puck?
questions.explanation: Name a change in D1 or F2 that could alter the plan. Saying where you would look is more useful than simply saying “scan.”

questions.prompt: What should you say before reaching the wall-side puck?

options.text: D1 is above me; F2 may be the inside outlet
D1 is inside, so I will check the wall-side support
F2 has drifted behind D1, so I will wait for a safer lane

questions.explanation: Naming D1 and F2 connects the actual pressure and outlet to the approach. If either moves, update the plan.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would make the first escape less useful?

options.text: D1 closes the inside lane
F2 is no longer reachable from control
The puck remains loose beside the wall

questions.explanation: Those named relationships remove the value of the first exit; protect the puck and find the next usable option.

questions.prompt: Move F2 to a middle support point that gives YOU a visible inside lane.
questions.explanation: This point moves F2 into a support relationship inside the wall-side retrieval; YOU can then check whether the lane is reachable.

questions.prompt: D1 arrives above the puck while F2 drifts behind coverage. How does your first action change?
questions.explanation: Connect the new pressure and lost outlet to a protected touch or wall-side escape, then name what you would scan before committing.

scenarios.title: Pressure behind the receiver
scenarios.objective: Prepare for a pass while checking pressure outside the receiver’s forward view.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 holds the puck and is preparing a pass toward YOU. YOU face F1; D1 waits behind your up-ice shoulder. F2 offers a different direction after reception.
cues: F1 has not released the puck.
YOU face the passer.
D1 is behind YOU relative to that facing.

questions.prompt: Who still owns the puck before the proposed pass?

options.text: F1
YOU
D1

questions.explanation: F1 is the designated carrier; YOU are preparing to receive.

questions.prompt: Which information matters before YOU turn up ice?

options.text: Whether D1 is closing
Whether F2 remains available
Whether the pass has actually reached your stick

questions.explanation: All three affect a turn or next pass. An intended reception must not be treated as completed possession.

questions.prompt: Order this receiving-and-next-read suggestion.

options.text: Check the space behind you
Receive the pass under control
Choose the next action using the updated space

questions.explanation: This routine separates preparation, possession and decision; another scan during reception may be useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a receiving spot that separates you from D1.
questions.explanation: The example opens a diagonal from F1 and more separation from D1. It is one option, not a required skating route.

questions.prompt: If D1 stays far back and the lane ahead remains open after reception, what becomes an option?

options.text: A controlled carry into that space
An automatic pass back every time
Turn up ice before confirming the pass arrived

questions.explanation: An open lane can support carrying. F2 or a return pass may still be useful if their evidence is better.

questions.prompt: Why is facing the passer not enough information for this reception?
questions.explanation: A receiver can see the puck while missing pressure from another direction. Explain what you would check and how it affects your next touch.

questions.prompt: What should YOU learn before F1 releases the pass?

options.text: Where D1 is and whether the wider shoulder is reachable
Which turn is mandatory
That F2 will receive next

questions.explanation: The pressure location and the reachable receiving shoulder explain why the reception can stay adaptable.

questions.prompt: Which two signs support receiving away from D1?

options.text: F1 can see the wider target
D1 remains inside rather than closing the target
F2 is up ice even if the pass lane is covered

questions.explanation: The passer's view and D1's position make the target useful; F2 is a later read.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a shoulder that opens F1's lane and leaves D1 inside.
questions.explanation: The changed angle separates YOU from D1 while preserving a route from F1.

questions.prompt: D1 reaches your inside shoulder as the puck arrives. Explain the changed reception and next scan.
questions.explanation: Protect the first touch away from D1, then scan whether F2 or a return lane remains. A turn is conditional on the space that is still there.

scenarios.title: Step out of the shaded lane
scenarios.objective: Recognize that a teammate can be nearby yet unavailable on a direct passing line.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 has possession. YOU are a nearby receiver, but D1 stands between you and the puck. F2 is farther across the ice. The task is to improve your own availability.
cues: D1 occupies the direct F1-to-YOU line.
F2 offers a separate angle.
Being nearest is different from having a clear lane.

questions.prompt: Which player stands on the direct line between F1 and YOU?

options.text: F2
D1
No player

questions.explanation: D1 sits between the carrier and your current receiving spot.

questions.prompt: What could make your support more useful?

options.text: Create a different angle from F1
Keep track of D1 as you move
Stand closer even if D1 stays in the same line

questions.explanation: Changing the angle can expose a lane. Closing distance alone does not remove the obstruction.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple re-offer routine.

options.text: Notice the blocked line
Move into a different passing angle
Check whether F1 can still see and reach you

questions.explanation: This is a suggested way to solve this obstruction; the carrier may choose another action meanwhile.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away from D1’s current passing shadow.
questions.explanation: The sample shifts across the line instead of only closer to F1. Other separated angles may work.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 follows your new route. What is a useful next read?

options.text: Assume the lane must still be open
Stay in the new spot without checking F1
Look for another angle or space opened for F2

questions.explanation: A defender’s response changes which lane is useful. Your movement can also help a teammate.

questions.prompt: How would you tell the difference between “closer” and “more available” here?
questions.explanation: Describe the carrier-to-receiver line and the defender in it, rather than relying only on distance.

questions.prompt: What is the useful communication after D1 blocks the first line?

options.text: I will re-offer above the line; check whether you can reach me
The first lane is open even if the picture changes
F2 must stay wide and never move

questions.explanation: The message names the changed angle and keeps F1's pass conditional on reachability.

questions.prompt: Which two responses could follow D1's reaction to your re-offer?

options.text: Use the new lane if F1 can reach it
Notice space D1 leaves for F2 if D1 follows
Pass to yourself through D1

questions.explanation: D1's response creates the next decision: use the lane, or exploit the space that the defender left.

questions.prompt: Move YOU across the blocked line into a visible support angle.
questions.explanation: This point changes the F1-to-YOU line and keeps F2 separate.

questions.prompt: F1 carries while D1 follows you. Explain the value of your movement.
questions.explanation: Your movement can pull D1 and open F2 or F1's carry lane. Call the open space, then re-check it because D1 may recover.

scenarios.title: A new job after your pass
scenarios.objective: Plan off-puck movement after a completed pass without assuming an immediate return.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU have just passed to F2, who now owns the puck. D1 lies between your old position and F2. This freeze begins after reception, not during flight.
cues: F2 owns the puck now.
YOU no longer need to carry it.
D1 shades the old return line.

questions.prompt: What changed when the stated pass finished?

options.text: YOU kept possession through the completed pass
F2 became the puck carrier
Both YOU and F2 now own the puck

questions.explanation: The briefing and ownership both identify F2 as the receiver in possession.

questions.prompt: Which choices keep YOU involved without owning the puck?

options.text: Offer a fresh return angle
Notice where D1 follows
Remain in the old return line without checking D1

questions.explanation: Off-puck support means remaining useful as the carrier and defence change.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested continuation after reception.

options.text: Recognize that F2 now has possession
Find space outside the old return line
Show a new option and read D1 again

questions.explanation: The routine begins from actual reception. It does not promise a second pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to offer a new return angle for F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves beyond the old obstruction. A shorter lateral option can also work if it creates a usable line.

questions.prompt: If F2 carries forward instead of returning the puck, what could YOU do?

options.text: Adjust support to F2’s new location
Insist that F2 pass back immediately
Stay at the original pass location without another look

questions.explanation: Support follows the actual carrier. The initial pass does not require a scripted return.

questions.prompt: What might your movement accomplish even if F2 never passes back?
questions.explanation: It could offer support, move a defender or leave another lane available. Identify which relationship you expect to change.

questions.prompt: After F2 receives, what should YOU communicate?

options.text: I am changing the support angle; tell me if the return lane opens
The puck must come straight back
My first pass is complete because I passed

questions.explanation: The message matches the new carrier and keeps the return conditional while support continues.

questions.prompt: Which two details decide where to support F2?

options.text: F2's direction with the puck
D1's coverage of the old return line
The fact that YOU passed once

questions.explanation: The current carrier and defender coverage describe the new job; the earlier pass does not fix the next spot.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a support point above the shaded return line.
questions.explanation: The point gives F2 a new relationship to read while keeping D1 visible.

questions.prompt: F2 carries toward the middle and D1 turns with F2. What do you do next?
questions.explanation: Match support to F2's new position, keep a usable lane, and communicate the space F1 or YOU can offer if D1 follows.

scenarios.title: An outlet behind half-wall pressure
scenarios.objective: Notice when a supporting player behind the carrier can offer a reset.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 owns the puck near the half wall, the side-board area partway into the attacking zone, and D1 is ahead of the carrier. YOU are also ahead of F1 but nearer the middle. Consider offering an option away from the forward pressure.
cues: The immediate pressure is ahead of F1.
YOU currently stand up ice of F1.
Space behind F1 is not occupied by a shown defender.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The reset is a conditional suggestion, not a command to pass backward in every pressured situation. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes YOU’s starting position?

options.text: Behind F1 toward the left end
Ahead of F1 toward the right end
Level with F1 toward the same goal line

questions.explanation: YOU have a larger x position than F1 while navy attacks +x.

questions.prompt: What should a reset outlet try to provide?

options.text: A line F1 can use
Separation from the pressuring defender
The closest possible position to the boards in every case

questions.explanation: A usable line and room matter; the still frame cannot guarantee future recovery times.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested support adjustment.

options.text: Notice the forward pressure
Offer a visible option behind it
Reassess after F1 chooses pass or carry

questions.explanation: Offering a reset adds an option without choosing F1’s action for them.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an outlet behind F1 with space from D1.
questions.explanation: The sample provides a diagonal back toward the middle. Other positions behind pressure may remain useful.

questions.prompt: Suppose D2 now moves into your reset lane. What would you reconsider?

options.text: Whether another angle or a protected hold is available
Whether the first reset must happen anyway
Whether the reset lane matters only before YOU move

questions.explanation: Recheck the new lane. A reset is useful only while the evidence supports it.

questions.prompt: What would make a backward pass helpful rather than just giving up ground?
questions.explanation: Explain what pressure it avoids and what options the new carrier might gain. Distance from the goal alone does not settle the decision.

questions.prompt: Why offer space behind F1 in this picture?

options.text: It can give F1 a reachable reset if pressure removes the forward lane
It gives F1 a reset even if D2 has taken that lane
It pulls YOU into D1's route

questions.explanation: The behind-pressure space is useful because F1 can choose it when reachable; the carrier may still carry or use another lane.

questions.prompt: Which two updates could cancel the reset?

options.text: D2 moves into the offered lane
F1 loses sight of YOU
D1 remains at the same spot

questions.explanation: D2 coverage or a lost sightline removes the reason for the reset; the unchanged D1 position alone does not decide it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU behind F1 with separation from both defenders.
questions.explanation: This reference places YOU behind F1 and away from D1, with D2 still visible for the next scan.

questions.prompt: D2 closes the reset while F1 still has the puck. Explain the next read.
questions.explanation: Name the closed reset, scan F1's remaining space and support, and choose carry, protection, or another outlet only if that lane remains usable.

scenarios.title: Find the loose rebound first
scenarios.objective: Separate a loose puck from a promised rebound goal.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The coach states that F1’s previous shot came loose to the goalie’s side. YOU are arriving away from the puck. No goal or next touch is assumed.
cues: The loose puck is on the positive-y side of the goal area.
D1 stands closer to the middle.
YOU must locate the puck before planning a second action.

questions.prompt: Where is the puck relative to the goalie at this freeze?

options.text: At centre ice
Off to one side of the goalie, still loose
Already in the goalie’s glove

questions.explanation: The puck is beside the goalie’s current area and has no owner. It is neither at centre ice nor held by the goalie.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter for your next approach?

options.text: Where the loose puck actually is
Where D1 is relative to the approach
The assumption that the next touch must be a shot

questions.explanation: Locate both puck and obstruction. A second chance still needs a real recovery and shooting opportunity.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested rebound-read routine.

options.text: Locate the loose puck
Check the approach and establish control if possible
Reassess a shot or pass

questions.explanation: This example emphasizes control and a new read. An immediate touch could be appropriate if the actual arrival supports it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to show an approach toward the loose-puck side.
questions.explanation: The example approaches from outside D1’s current middle position. It is not proof that YOU arrive first.

questions.prompt: If the goalie covers the puck before YOU arrive, what changes?

options.text: The puck is still available for a rebound shot
YOU can assume a goal
The previous loose-puck plan no longer applies

questions.explanation: A covered puck is a different state. Do not continue acting on the earlier loose-puck assumption.

questions.prompt: What extra information would you need before predicting a second shot?
questions.explanation: You might need puck movement, defender speed, control and whether play is still active. A static loose puck does not establish them.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while approaching the rebound?

options.text: Puck below the circle; D1 is between it and the net
The second shot is ours
F1 must shoot next

questions.explanation: The call names the actual puck and defender, which helps F1 understand the recovery read.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would alter the rebound plan?

options.text: D1 controls the puck
F1 becomes a reachable support option
The net stays at the same end

questions.explanation: Possession and support change the next job; the net location alone does not decide the play.

questions.prompt: Move YOU below the puck on its net-side approach.
questions.explanation: This point approaches the loose puck while preserving D1 and the net in view.

questions.prompt: The goalie covers before you arrive. What do you re-read?
questions.explanation: The loose-puck option is gone, so identify who has the puck and where F1 can support before choosing the next pressure or reset.

scenarios.title: Keep the puck away from pressure
scenarios.objective: Connect puck-side space and nearby pressure when planning a protected carry.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU own the puck near the side boards. D1 approaches from the middle side and F2 is an outlet inside. This is a no-contact planning exercise.
cues: D1 approaches from the middle side.
The puck is currently on YOU’s wall side.
F2 offers a separate inside target.

questions.prompt: Which shown player is the immediate opponent near YOU?

options.text: D1
F2

questions.prompt: What would help preserve options during this carry?

options.text: Notice D1’s reach and movement
Keep checking whether F2 is available
Watch only the puck for the whole play

questions.explanation: Protection and awareness work together. The picture does not prescribe a particular hand or body technique.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested pressure response.

options.text: Notice which side D1 threatens
Keep control while using available space
Recheck the outlet or escape

questions.explanation: This discussion sequence is conditional; on ice the actions can overlap.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a possible holding spot away from D1’s current approach.
questions.explanation: The example creates separation toward the wall without leaving the ice. It is not a required reverse or a guaranteed escape.

questions.prompt: If D1 follows toward the wall and F2’s lane opens, what becomes worth checking?

options.text: Whether an inside pass is now usable
Whether staying at the boards is always required
Whether F2’s earlier position still guarantees an outlet

questions.explanation: Pressure can change the outlet. A pass still depends on control and a clear actual lane.

questions.prompt: How could protecting the puck help F2 become useful?
questions.explanation: It may keep possession long enough for an outlet to appear. Explain the defender or passing-line change you would watch.

questions.prompt: What communication matches this protected carry?

options.text: D1 is inside; F2 may open if D1 follows
I will carry outside even if the picture changes
F2 must stop moving

questions.explanation: The call connects D1's approach to F2's conditional availability.

questions.prompt: Which two cues support holding the outside shoulder?

options.text: D1 stays inside YOU
F2 can be reached from the protected touch
The wall itself makes the puck safe

questions.explanation: The defender side and F2 lane explain the protection; the wall does not guarantee safety.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the outside while keeping F2 inside the picture.
questions.explanation: This point changes the pressure angle and leaves F2 visible.

questions.prompt: D1 follows outside and F2 opens. Explain the next decision.
questions.explanation: Name D1's movement and check F2's reachable lane. Pass only if that route remains open; otherwise protect again.

scenarios.title: Space to carry before the defender arrives
scenarios.objective: Recognize room for a controlled carry without assuming speed from a frozen pose.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU carry in the neutral area. D1 is offset toward the middle and F2 is farther up the same wide side. Speed is not shown; imagine choosing a controlled next route.
cues: D1 is offset from the direct wide lane.
F2 is ahead on the wide side.
The freeze supplies positions, not speeds.

questions.prompt: What can this neutral-zone freeze tell you directly?

options.text: YOU’s exact skating speed
The players’ relative locations
Which skater will win the race

questions.prompt: Which cues could change a carry decision?

options.text: D1 moving into your route
F2 moving into a useful receiving lane
The camera rotating while players stay fixed

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested open-space read.

options.text: Find an available route
Carry under control while observing D1
Choose again as the gap changes

questions.explanation: The routine requires updating the read, rather than promising that an initially open route stays open.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a possible next wide carrying position.
questions.explanation: The example advances without going directly toward D1. It represents a planned destination, not an instantaneous teleport.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 turns and reaches the wide lane before you do. What could YOU change?

options.text: Keep the route because it was open earlier
Reconsider pace, direction or F2’s outlet
Assume F2 will remain available without checking

questions.prompt: What movement would you watch to decide whether to keep carrying?
questions.explanation: Identify a change in D1’s path or F2’s availability and explain how it would alter your plan.

questions.prompt: What would you tell F2 during the open carry?

options.text: I have room now; show me if D1 closes the lane
The carry is certain to work
Stay wide even if D1 arrives

questions.explanation: The message reports the visible space and makes the next cue conditional.

questions.prompt: Which two updates should follow D1's turn?

options.text: The lane ahead of YOU
F2's availability on the wide side
The original open-space label

questions.explanation: D1's turn and F2's current lane determine whether the carry continues.

questions.prompt: Move YOU farther into the forward lane before D1 closes.
questions.explanation: This point moves into the shown open lane and leaves F2 on the outside.

questions.prompt: D1 reaches the wide lane. How do you keep the play alive?

scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU carry through the neutral zone toward F2 and D1. F2 occupies your straight path; D1 is closer to the middle. This exercise plans a turn, not a collision or contact play.
cues: F2 occupies the straight-ahead route.
D1 is on the middle side.
The positive-y side has room in this freeze.

questions.prompt: Which teammate occupies the straight-ahead route from YOU?

options.text: F2
D1
Nobody

questions.explanation: F2 is directly ahead at the same y position. D1 is an opponent offset toward the middle.

questions.prompt: What belongs in this turning decision?

options.text: Room beside the traffic
How much speed and control YOU actually have
The assumption that a teammate cannot obstruct a route

questions.explanation: A useful plan considers both available space and the movement the still picture cannot show.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested controlled-turn plan.

options.text: Notice the traffic before reaching it
Choose a turn you can control
Look again as you leave the turn

questions.explanation: The order is a planning aid. It does not teach a particular edge technique from a static model.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a possible turning space beside the traffic.
questions.explanation: The example uses the wall-side room short of F2. Another controlled route could work if D1’s movement allows it.

questions.prompt: Suppose F2 moves toward that same outside space. What would help now?

options.text: Keep the planned turn without another look
Reassess space and slow or choose another route
Aim at F2’s original empty spot without checking D1

questions.explanation: Both traffic and available routes changed. Speed control or a different turn can be safer and more useful.

questions.prompt: Why must a turning plan account for a teammate as well as D1?
questions.explanation: A teammate can occupy the route even without defending it. Explain how you would preserve room for both players.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before turning?

options.text: F2 is ahead; I am checking the side space around D1
The outside lane is mine even if the picture changes
D1 does not affect the turn

questions.explanation: The call identifies both traffic cues and leaves the turn adaptable.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would make the first turn poor?

options.text: F2 moves into the side space
D1 closes the turn lane
YOU still sees the puck

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a side-space entry that avoids F2 and D1.
questions.explanation: This point changes the turn angle while leaving both players visible.

questions.prompt: F2 enters the side space as you begin turning. Explain your adjustment.
questions.explanation: Do not crowd F2. Protect the puck, choose another angle, and re-check D1 before continuing.
